How is Billings laid out, and why does it matter for a house sale?

Billings sits in the Yellowstone Valley at 3,126 feet and is split by the Rims, a line of sandstone cliffs also called the Rimrocks. According to Wikipedia's summary of Census data, the city covers about 43.5 square miles of land, with two-thirds in the Yellowstone Valley and the South Hills and one-third in the Heights and Lockwood area.

The cliffs run north and east of downtown. The northern face is about 500 feet tall and the eastern face about 800 feet, which separates downtown from the Heights to the north and Lockwood to the east. Billings Logan International Airport sits on top of the Rims.

  • Downtown and the valley floor: older housing near the Yellowstone River.
  • Billings Heights: north of the Rims, along U.S. Highway 87, called Main Street inside the city.
  • Lockwood: east of downtown, linked to the Heights by the planned Billings Bypass.
  • South Hills, West End and Shiloh: reached by Interstate 90 and Montana Highway 3.

The cliffs also make the Rimrocks a landmark. Billings has more than 50 miles of trails in and around the city, including about seven continuous miles along the top of the Rims, and seven mountain ranges are visible from town. A house with a view of the Rims or an easy route onto the trail system has features a listing can point to.

What is the history behind Billings, Montana?

Billings was founded in 1877 and incorporated on March 24, 1882. It is named for Frederick H. Billings, a former president of the Northern Pacific Railroad. The area was earlier known as Clark's Fork Bottom.

The first town in the Yellowstone Valley was Coulson, formed in 1877 around a sawmill and a trading post. When the Northern Pacific came through, the railroad owned two adjoining sections about two miles west of Coulson and chose to build a new town there. Most Coulson residents gradually moved to the new town, and Boothill Cemetery is the only physical trace left of Coulson.

The Crow have lived in the Billings area since about 1700, and the present-day Crow Nation lies just south of the city. William Clark passed through in July 1806 and carved his name on Pompey's Pillar east of town.

What does the Billings economy look like?

Healthcare is the largest employment sector. Billings Clinic employs about 4,500 people and St. Vincent Regional Hospital about 2,200, and together they anchor a growing medical corridor.

How does Billings weather affect an older house?

Billings has a cold semi-arid climate with hot, dry summers and cold, dry winters. Snowfall averages 57.4 inches a year, but warm chinook winds mean snow does not usually stay long. The snowiest year on record was 2017 to 2018, at 106.1 inches.

  • Temperatures reach 100 degrees on an average of 1 to 3 days a year and fall below 0 on about 12.9 days.
  • The first freeze of the season arrives by about October 6 and the last by about May 5.
  • On June 20, 2010, a tornado touched down in the Heights and downtown with hail up to golf ball size, and it severely damaged the MetraPark Arena.

Hail is the item for roof inspections. A buyer's inspector may flag aging shingles, and a seller who wants to skip a repair negotiation can sell the house as is.

What schools and roads serve Billings?

Billings Public Schools includes the Billings Elementary and Billings High School districts, with 21 elementary schools, six middle schools and three high schools: Senior High, Skyview High and West High. Other elementary districts that cover parts of Billings are Blue Creek, Elder Grove, Canyon Creek, Elysian and Independent.

Interstate 90 runs east to west through the south of the city, and Interstate 94 meets it east of downtown. U.S. 87 through the Heights is described as the busiest section of roadway in Montana. The Billings Bypass is planned to link the Heights and Lockwood, and its new Yellowstone River bridge was completed in 2023.

Montana State University Billings, founded in 1927 as a normal school and known as Eastern Montana College from 1949 to 1994, enrolls around 4,100 students. Private options include Billings Catholic Schools, with about 1,000 students, and Billings Christian School.

Billings METropolitan Transit runs fixed-route and paratransit buses, with downtown and West End transit centers. Amtrak's North Coast Hiawatha last stopped at the Billings Depot in 1979.

How is property tax handled in Billings and Yellowstone County?

Billings homes are taxed through the Yellowstone County Treasurer, currently Hank Peters, at 2825 3rd Avenue North, Room 113, phone 406-256-2802. The county says the department collects about $345 million a year and processes roughly 75,000 real estate, 5,900 mobile home and 1,050 personal property tax bills.

The Department of Revenue's 2026 rates give primary residences and long-term rentals a tiered scale beginning at 0.76% on the first $378,000, while second homes, short-term rentals and vacant lots pay 1.90%. An owner who disagrees with a valuation has 30 days from the notice date to file Form AB-26, or may appeal directly to the county tax appeal board.

What are the ways to sell a house in Billings?

There are three routes: list with an agent, sell it yourself, or accept a cash offer. Each carries different costs, timelines and risks under Montana law.

  • List with an agent: exposure to more buyers, plus commission, showings and repairs a buyer's inspection may request.
  • Sell it yourself: you save commission and handle the marketing, contract and paperwork.
  • Cash offer: a direct purchase, usually as is, with a closing date you choose.

Whichever route you take, the deed has to be acknowledged and recorded with the county clerk and recorder, a Realty Transfer Certificate has to accompany it, and the standard recording fee is $20 for the first page and $10 for each added page. Any unpaid property tax is a lien on the house and gets paid at closing.

If you want a cash offer on a Billings house, tell us about the property in the form above. We reply with a written offer, and you owe nothing if you turn it down.

What paperwork closes a house sale in Billings?

The closing file for a Billings house includes a deed, a Realty Transfer Certificate and the recording fee, all filed with the county clerk and recorder. The Department of Revenue says the certificate collects sale price information used in the mass appraisal of Montana real property, so the price you report can show up later in how nearby homes are valued.

  • Seller and buyer names must match on the certificate and the deed.
  • The certificate asks for the last four digits of each party's Social Security or employer identification number.
  • The deed must be acknowledged before a notary before it can be recorded.

Once recorded, the deed is constructive notice to later buyers and lenders from the time of filing.

More questions about Billings, MT

How big is Billings, Montana?

The 2025 Census Bureau estimate is 121,239 residents. The city covers about 43.5 square miles of land and sits at 3,126 feet in the Yellowstone Valley.

When are Yellowstone County property taxes due?

The first half of real estate tax is due November 30, with December 3 as the 2026 date, and the second half is due May 31, with June 1 in 2027. Payments are due by 5 p.m. Mountain Time.

Who is the largest employer in Billings?

Healthcare is the largest sector. Billings Clinic employs about 4,500 people and St. Vincent Regional Hospital about 2,200.

Does Billings get hail?

Yes. A June 20, 2010 tornado came with hail up to golf ball size and damaged downtown, the Heights and the MetraPark Arena. Roof condition is a common point in a Billings sale.

Can I sell my Billings house as is?

Yes. A cash buyer can purchase a Billings house in its present condition, and the sale still requires a recorded deed and a Realty Transfer Certificate.

Where is Missoula, and what does that mean for selling a house here?

Missoula is the county seat of Missoula County in western Montana, set along the Clark Fork River near where the Bitterroot and Blackfoot rivers join it. It sits at the meeting point of five mountain ranges, which is why people often call it the hub of five valleys.

The city covers about 35 square miles and sits at an elevation of 3,209 feet. Mount Sentinel and Mount Jumbo rise right beside town, so many streets run up against hillsides. A house on a slope can carry different drainage, access and foundation questions than one on the valley floor, and buyers ask about that early.

Idaho is less than 25 miles to the west. North Reserve Street, at the crossing of Highway 93 and the old Mullan Road with easy access to Interstate 90, became the main retail district in the late 1990s. Sellers near the university or old downtown are in a different pocket of town, with older homes and tighter lots.

What shaped Missoula's economy, and who employs people here?

Missoula grew from a sawmill settlement into a college and health care town. Mills supplied settlers on the Mullan Road, Fort Missoula opened in 1877, and the Northern Pacific Railway arrived in 1883, which pushed the lumber industry along.

The Montana Legislature picked Missoula for the state's first university in 1893, and a U.S. Forest Service headquarters followed in 1908. Lumber and the university carried the local economy for roughly the next 100 years. The lumber side then wound down: a plywood plant in Bonner closed in 2007, the Bonner sawmill in 2008, and the Smurfit-Stone pulp mill in 2010.

Today the largest employers named in published summaries are the University of Montana, Missoula County Public Schools and the city's two hospitals, St. Patrick Hospital and Community Medical Center. St. Patrick is described as the only Level II trauma center in western Montana. Those anchors matter to a seller because they keep a steady base of renters, staff and students looking for housing near campus and the hospitals.

  • University of Montana, chartered in 1893 and open since 1895
  • St. Patrick Hospital, founded in 1873
  • Community Medical Center
  • Missoula County Public Schools

How does Missoula's climate affect a house you want to sell?

Missoula has a humid continental climate with cold, moderately snowy winters and hot, dry summers. Winter snowfall averages 39.5 inches, usually between October 30 and April 20, and the ground holds snow for about 120 days a year.

That snow load is the main thing an inspector looks at on a roof. Older roofs with sagging decking, poor attic ventilation or ice dams show up quickly in a Missoula inspection. Heating systems get close attention too. The coldest month, December, averages 23.9 degrees, and the record low is minus 33 degrees from January 1957.

Summer matters as well. Missoula averages 24 days a year at or above 90 degrees, and the record high is 107 degrees, set most recently on June 30, 2021. Homes without air conditioning, which are common in older neighborhoods, can feel that in a showing.

The city also sits beside rivers. Anyone selling near the Clark Fork or Bitterroot should check the county floodplain maps before listing.

When are Missoula property taxes due, and what happens if they are late?

Missoula County real property taxes are due on or before the last day of November and May each year. If that day falls on a weekend or holiday, the due date moves to the next business day, unless you received help through the Montana Department of Revenue's assistance program.

Bills go out in late October or early November. Both halves appear on one invoice, and the county does not mail a separate second-half bill. You can pay online, in person at the Treasurer's Office or by mail, and a mailed payment has to be postmarked by the due date.

Late payments carry a 2% penalty and interest at a 10% annual rate, according to the county. The county then moves through a set calendar:

  • Late June or early July: delinquent notices go out.
  • First business day of August: a tax lien attaches, with a $75 lien certificate fee.
  • Late August: outside investors may buy the lien.
  • After the lien attaches, the owner has two to three years to pay before risking the property.

For a seller this means unpaid tax is not a reason to panic, but it must be cleared at or before closing. Ask the title company for a payoff figure and compare it with the county's online tax lookup. You can read the county's own rules on its property tax questions page.

How do I dispute a Missoula property valuation?

The Montana Department of Revenue, not the county, sets the value of your home, and it reappraises residential property every two years. If you disagree, you file an appeal when the notice arrives.

There are two paths. You can send the department a Request for Informal Classification and Appraisal Review, known as Form AB-26, or you can appeal directly to the Missoula County Tax Appeal Board. Both are filed through the state's tax appeal website. Yellowstone County's board explains the timing under state law: an objection made within 30 days of the date on the notice applies to both years of the two-year cycle, while a later one applies only to the second year, with a June 1 limit.

That timing is worth knowing if you plan to sell. A lower value can reduce your remaining tax bill, but an appeal does not change what you owe at closing until it is decided. Pay what is billed and let the title company prorate it.

Your property record card is public. The state publishes the characteristics, buildings and land details online, and checking it for errors in square footage or bedroom count is a quick first step.

What building permit rules should a Missoula seller know about?

The City of Missoula requires permits for new one and two unit dwellings, and those must follow the International Residential Code. Smaller projects have exemptions, such as free-standing residential decks that are 30 inches or less above the ground.

Work done without a permit is the problem sellers run into. Missoula's Development Services page lists a section on work without a permit, and a buyer's inspector or lender may ask for permit history on a finished basement, an addition or a converted garage. The city's Zoning Desk can be reached by email or by phone between 10 am and 2 pm at (406) 552-6625.

Property outside city limits falls under Missoula County, which runs its own permit guide at missoulacounty.build. Check which one applies to your address before you start any repair.

  • Find the parcel on the county property information system.
  • Ask whether past additions were permitted.

How do Missoula sellers usually get around, and does it affect the sale?

Mountain Line operates 14 bus routes covering Missoula, East Missoula, Bonner, Target Range, Rattlesnake and the airport, plus paratransit and four park and ride lots.

Missoula Montana Airport, run by the Missoula County Airport Authority, is the largest in western Montana. Relocation is common here because of the university and hospitals.

Passenger rail ended in 1979 when Amtrak dropped the North Coast Hiawatha. The Northern Pacific depot at the end of Higgins Avenue is on the National Register of Historic Places.

What do sellers in Missoula usually run into?

Sellers here tend to face a handful of repeat issues, and most of them come from the age of the housing and the mix of owners and renters.

  • Roofs and attics worn by decades of snow load.
  • Older homes near campus with deferred maintenance.
  • Inherited houses that need a probate step before they can transfer.
  • Tax bills split across several districts, including city, county, fire and water.
  • Slope, drainage or floodplain questions that come up late in escrow.

A cash purchase can shorten the list because the buyer is not relying on a lender's appraisal, but price and terms still depend on the house. We make offers case by case, and you are free to compare them with a listing. Whichever route you take, get a title commitment early so liens and tax items are known.

The recorder side of the county office handles deeds and property records. Missoula County's Clerk and Recorder keeps deeds, surveys and land books searchable online, which helps you confirm the legal description and any easements on your lot.

More questions about Missoula, MT

When are property taxes due in Missoula County?

Real property taxes are due on or before the last day of November and May. If that date lands on a weekend or holiday, the next business day applies. Both halves come on a single bill mailed in late October or early November.

What is the penalty for late property tax in Missoula?

The county charges a 2% penalty plus interest at a 10% annual rate on delinquent taxes. A lien attaches on the first business day of August, and the owner then has two to three years to pay before risking the property.

Who sets my home's value in Missoula?

The Montana Department of Revenue sets it, and it reappraises residential property every two years. You can request an informal review with Form AB-26 or appeal to the Missoula County Tax Appeal Board.

Does a Missoula house need a permit for a deck?

Not always. The city says a residential deck needs no permit if it is free-standing and 30 inches or less above the ground, among other criteria. Anything attached or taller should be checked with Development Services.

Can I sell a Missoula house with an unpaid tax bill?

Yes. Unpaid taxes are paid from the sale proceeds at closing, and the title company will request a payoff figure from the Treasurer. Resolving it before you list avoids surprises.

How much snow does Missoula get, and why does it matter for a sale?

Winter snowfall averages 39.5 inches, with snow on the ground about 120 days a year. Buyers and inspectors look closely at roof condition, ventilation and heating because of that load.

Where is Great Falls and why is it called the Electric City?

Great Falls is the county seat of Cascade County in central Montana and the third most populous city in the state. The 2020 census counted 60,442 residents in 22.9 square miles, and the metro area, which covers all of Cascade County, had 84,414.

The city sits just east of the Rocky Mountains and the Missouri River runs through it. It is named for a series of five waterfalls on the river, and three of them, Black Eagle, Rainbow and the Great Falls itself, host hydroelectric dams. That is where the "Electric City" nickname comes from. Interstate 15 serves the city from the north and south, and Great Falls International Airport sits on the west side next to the Montana Air National Guard.

How did Great Falls get started?

Great Falls was planned as an industrial city. Paris Gibson visited the falls in 1880, saw the potential for cheap hydropower, and returned in 1883 to plat a settlement on the south side of the river. James J. Hill's Great Northern Railway arrived in October 1887, and the city was incorporated on November 28, 1888.

Black Eagle Dam was completed in 1890 and was the first hydroelectric dam built in Montana. A smelter went up in nearby Black Eagle the same year. Early buildings from that era still stand, including the former Central High School, finished in 1896, and the Cascade County Courthouse of 1903. Much of the early city was built around the railroad and smelter economy, so ask your buyer how they view an older house near downtown or the river.

What does Malmstrom Air Force Base mean for the local housing market?

Malmstrom is the largest employer in the Great Falls community, and its workforce shapes demand for houses. The base reports about 3,371 active-duty members and 525 Department of the Air Force civilians, with about 3,300 family members living on or near the base. Its annual economic impact for fiscal year 2025 was approximately $444 million, and it accounted for 959 indirect jobs.

Malmstrom is one of three Air Force bases that operate the Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missile, under the 341st Missile Wing. The base sits east of the city, and an estimated 6,500 veterans live in the local area.

Military assignments run on a cycle, and a family with orders can face a short window to move. A sale that depends on a buyer's loan approval can feel slow in that situation.

  • If you have orders, share your report date with any buyer or agent at the start.
  • Ask how much time a cash closing needs compared with a financed one.
  • Tell the buyer whether the house is vacant, since that can affect the closing date.

What is the weather like in Great Falls, and what does it do to a roof and a furnace?

Great Falls has a cold semi-arid climate with long, often snowy winters, hot dry summers and a notable amount of summer thunderstorm rain. The wettest part of the year is spring. Chinook winds can warm the winter: afternoons above 50 degrees Fahrenheit average about fifteen across the three winter months.

The swings are large. There are on average 20.8 nights a year at 0 degrees or colder and 44 days that never rise above freezing, and highs reach 90 degrees on about nineteen days. The daily range often exceeds 30 degrees. In August 1992 a two-day snowfall totaled 8.3 inches.

A house takes this in several ways. Repeated freeze and thaw works on foundations and driveways. Roofs carry snowy winters and summer thunderstorms. Furnaces and water heaters carry long heating seasons. If you know a roof is past its age or a furnace is shaky, say so in your disclosure, because buyers will find it.

How does code enforcement work in Great Falls?

Great Falls enforces its property code mainly in response to complaints. The city describes code enforcement as complaint-driven, covering rubbish, junk vehicles and property maintenance issues. For private property, the contact is Planning and Community Development at 406-455-8574. In the public right-of-way, call Public Works at 406-771-1401.

If neighbors have complained about your yard, an open code case on the house can complicate a sale. Clear it before you list, or tell the buyer what is open. The city also has nine neighborhood councils, which are a useful place to learn what is happening on your street.

How are Great Falls property taxes billed?

Cascade County bills and collects the tax, and the schedule follows state law. Residential bills are usually mailed in late October. The first payment is due November 30, or within 30 days of the postmark if that is later, and the second is due May 31. Residential property is valued every two years at 100 percent of market value.

For the 2025 tax year, Montana changed the way it taxes homes. The rate is 0.76 percent on the first $400,000 of market value, 1.10 percent on the portion up to $1.5 million, and 2.20 percent above that, as set out on the Department of Revenue's 2025 information page. The Cascade County property tax office is at 121 4th Street North, Suite 1A, and its phone number is 406-454-6850.

At closing, any unpaid tax for the current period is normally settled through the title company. Ask for a payoff figure so you know the amount before you sign.

What must a seller tell the buyer in Montana?

A Great Falls seller has to hand over a disclosure statement covering adverse material facts the seller actually knows. Section 70-20-502 of the Montana Code lists title issues, water and wastewater systems, structural and mechanical problems, additions without a building permit, hazardous materials, drainage and soil problems, and testing for radon, mold, lead-based paint and similar items.

The statement has to be delivered before or with the contract. If it comes later, the buyer can rescind within three days under section 70-20-504. The duty is lighter for transfers ordered by a court, foreclosure sales, transfers to a spouse, child or parent, and transfers between co-owners, all of which are listed in section 70-20-503.

What choices do Great Falls homeowners have when they need to sell?

There are three realistic routes, and the best one depends on the condition of the house and on how soon you need to close.

  • A traditional listing. This puts the house in front of the most buyers. Expect showings, an inspection and a buyer with a loan, which adds time and sometimes repair requests.
  • A for-sale-by-owner sale. You save the agent's commission, but you carry the marketing, negotiation and disclosure paperwork.
  • A cash sale to a company that buys houses. The buyer takes the property as it is, there is no loan to approve, and the closing date can be set around your move. The price reflects the repairs and risk the buyer takes on, so compare the written offer to your expected net from a listing.

No cash offer is guaranteed. A buyer needs to see the house and the title before putting a number on it.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What problems do sellers in Great Falls commonly face?

  • A military move with a fixed report date.
  • An older house near the river or downtown with aging wiring, plumbing or a roof near the end of its life.
  • An inherited house shared by several heirs, some out of state.
  • An open code complaint over junk, rubbish or an unmaintained yard.
  • A rental with tenants or deferred repairs that the owner no longer wants to manage.

More questions about Great Falls, MT

How fast can I sell a house in Great Falls?

Timing depends on the title, the buyer and how ready you are. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and loan approval, which are the steps that often slow a financed sale.

Do I need to fix a Great Falls house before selling it for cash?

No. A cash buyer purchases the house as it is. You still must disclose problems you know about under Montana law.

Who do I call about a code complaint on my Great Falls property?

For private property, call Planning and Community Development at 406-455-8574. For the public right-of-way, call Public Works at 406-771-1401.

When are Cascade County property taxes due?

The first half is due November 30, or within 30 days of the postmark if that is later, and the second half is due May 31. The county property tax office can be reached at 406-454-6850.

Is the Malmstrom workforce a reason Great Falls homes sell quickly?

Malmstrom is the largest employer in the community, and the base reports about 3,300 family members on or near it. How quickly any one house sells still depends on its condition, location and price.

Where is Bozeman, Montana, and how is the area set up?

Bozeman is in Gallatin County, in the Gallatin Valley of southwest Montana, at 4,817 feet. It is 84 miles east of Butte, 125 miles west of Billings and 93 miles north of Yellowstone National Park, and Interstate 90 passes through it.

The Bridger Mountains rise to the north-northeast, the Hyalite Peaks of the Gallatin Range to the south, the Spanish Peaks of the Madison Range to the south-southwest and the Tobacco Root Mountains to the west-southwest. The city's land area is about 20.9 square miles, according to Census Bureau figures reported by Wikipedia.

The 2020 census counted 53,293 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 58,814. The metro area is about 118,960. The city government runs a Community Housing Program, covered below.

What is the history of Bozeman?

John Bozeman opened the Bozeman Trail in 1863, a branch off the Oregon Trail leading to the mining town of Virginia City through the Gallatin Valley. He platted the town with Daniel Rouse and William Beall in August 1864.

  • 1806: William Clark camped east of the future city at the mouth of Kelly Canyon.
  • 1867: Fort Ellis was established nearby.
  • 1883: Bozeman incorporated, with a city council form of government.
  • 1922: Voters adopted the commission and city manager form that the city still uses.

Nelson Story drove about 1,000 head of Longhorn cattle into Paradise Valley in 1866 and later donated land to the state for Montana State University. The valley was called the Valley of the Flowers, and the Crow people held much of it as territory.

What drives the Bozeman economy?

Bozeman's top employers include Bozeman Health, Montana State University, Simms Fishing Products and Mystery Ranch. The city also has at least two dozen high-tech firms working on lasers and optical equipment, over a dozen biotech companies and several large software companies.

How does Bozeman's climate affect a house?

Bozeman has a humid continental climate. It receives up to 24 inches of precipitation a year, compared with 8 to 12 inches across much of Montana east of the Continental Divide. That moisture helped give the Gallatin Valley its lush plant growth, which Wikipedia says likely contributed to the choice of Bozeman for Montana State, the state's agricultural college.

  • Winters are cold and snowy, and summers are relatively warm.
  • At this elevation the swing between day and night temperatures can be large.
  • The record high was 105 degrees on July 31, 1892, and the record low was minus 46 degrees, set in 1957 and 1983.

For a seller, snow load on the roof, ice at the eaves and the condition of exterior wood are normal points for a buyer's inspector to check. A house with deferred repairs can be sold as is to a cash buyer rather than repaired before listing.

Almost all of Bozeman is in Bozeman Elementary School District and Bozeman High School District, and a small piece extends into Belgrade's districts. Bozeman Public Schools operates two high schools, Bozeman High and Gallatin High, two middle schools, Chief Joseph and Sacajawea, and eight elementary schools: Emily Dickinson, Hawthorne, Hyalite, Irving, Longfellow, Meadowlark, Morning Star and Whittier.

Interstate 90, U.S. Highway 191 and Montana Highways 86 and 84 are the main roads. Streamline, a zero-fare bus system, was run by the Human Resource Development Council from 2006 until July 1, 2025, when the new Gallatin Valley Urban Transportation District took over. The Skyline bus links Bozeman and Big Sky, and Bozeman Yellowstone International Airport serves travelers to Big Sky, West Yellowstone and Yellowstone National Park.

The Bozeman Fire Department is a full-time career department with 47 uniformed firefighters at three stations, and it responded to about 5,000 emergency calls in 2020.

What is the housing picture in Bozeman?

The City of Bozeman describes housing as a complex challenge that no single program can solve. Its Community Housing Program aims to expand options for people who live, work and study in the city, and it publishes housing data and help resources on its website.

The Regional Housing Coalition's report, Bridging the Gap: A Guide to Funding Affordable Housing in Montana, looks at funding sources for affordable housing in Gallatin County, including tools available locally and ones that would need state action. The program page lists the people it serves: local workers, families, students, seniors, renters, future homeowners and neighborhoods.

The office is at 311 West Main, Room 103, Bozeman, and can be reached at 406-582-3030 or treasurer@gallatin.mt.gov, Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. The Department of Revenue's Bozeman office, 406-582-3400, handles questions on market and taxable value.

Where is Butte, and how is the city set up?

Butte is the county seat of Silver Bow County in southwestern Montana, and the city and county run as one government. The city and county governments consolidated in 1977 to form Butte-Silver Bow, which covers about 718 square miles. That is far more ground than the dense urban core, so a house sold under a "Butte" address can sit on a steep Uptown street or on open land out toward the edge of the county.

The city sits in the Silver Bow Creek Valley on the Continental Divide. Every highway leaving town except westbound I-90 crosses the Divide, and Butte is one of only two Montana cities where two interstates meet: I-15 runs north and south, I-90 runs east and west. Bert Mooney Airport has commercial flights on Delta Connection. The 2020 census counted 34,494 residents, which made Butte the fifth-largest city in the state.

What in Butte's history still affects a house today?

Butte began as a mining camp in 1864 and grew into one of the largest copper boom towns in the American West. Workers arrived from Ireland, Cornwall, Wales, Italy, Finland, Montenegro, China and many other places, and they built neighborhoods around the mines. Names like Dublin Gulch, Meaderville and the McQueen Addition come from that period.

The mines did not stay in the background. The Berkeley Pit opened in 1954, and Wikipedia's history of the city notes that thousands of homes in Meaderville, McQueen and East Butte were removed to make room for it. Mining in the pit was suspended in 1983 and ended for good in 1985. Butte's economy since 2000 has leaned on energy companies such as NorthWestern Energy, on healthcare, and on Montana Technological University, a public engineering school in town.

You can still see the old industry from a residential street. Butte's urban landscape includes mining headframes set within neighborhoods, and the Uptown Historic District holds nearly 6,000 contributing properties. Some Butte houses date from that era, and a buyer will want to know what has been updated.

What does the Butte Superfund cleanup mean for someone selling a house?

It means your yard may be tested for lead, and the testing area just grew. On September 21, 2026, the EPA finalized a Record of Decision Amendment for the Butte Priority Soils Operable Unit. The amendment lowers the residential soil-lead cleanup level from 1,200 parts per million to 456 ppm and expands the Residential Metals Abatement Program area by about 3,627 acres. Over 7,000 more properties now qualify for assessment and, if needed, cleanup.

Under the selected remedy, a property is divided into decision units such as the front yard, back yard, play area and driveway. Each unit is sampled, and any unit above 456 ppm is excavated and replaced with clean fill. Properties that were sampled earlier and passed under the old 1,200 ppm level will be reevaluated. EPA expects the sampling and cleanup in the expanded area to take roughly 15 years from 2026.

Here is what that can look like for a seller:

  • A buyer may ask whether your lot has been sampled and what the result was.
  • A yard that passed before may be looked at again under the lower level.
  • Cleanup work is done on the property by the program, so ask the program what applies to your address before you list.
  • Under Montana law you must disclose known adverse material facts, which includes any testing or treatment for lead-based paint or contaminated soil that you know about.

A cash buyer who works in Butte will already know about the program. That can shorten the conversation, because the buyer prices the question in rather than discovering it during an inspection.

How does Butte weather treat an older house?

Butte has a cold semi-arid climate with long winters, and the weather is the main source of repair bills. January averages 20.0 degrees Fahrenheit, and in a typical year about 31 nights fall below 0 degrees. About 54 days never climb above freezing. Summers are short, with warm days and cool nights: July averages 63.6 degrees.

Precipitation is low and comes mostly in spring. The driest calendar year on record was 2021, with 6.49 inches. Snowfall is limited by the dryness, but the deepest snow on the ground reached 27 inches in December 1996. For a house, the long cold season puts heavy demand on heating systems, roofs and plumbing, so those are the items a buyer's inspector is likely to check first.

Do historic rules apply if I sell or demolish a Butte house?

They can. The Butte-Silver Bow Historic Preservation Commission reviews demolition permits for historic properties anywhere in the county except Walkerville. Butte Citizens for Preservation and Revitalization describes the commission's role as including design review for properties on the Local Register and for properties that receive local funds or tax credits.

That matters if you own a deteriorated Uptown building and a buyer plans to tear it down or alter it. A sale itself does not trigger review, but the buyer's plans can. If your house is on the Local Register or inside a historic district, tell any buyer early so the deal does not stall at the permit counter.

How does property tax work in Butte-Silver Bow?

Real estate tax is billed once a year and paid in two halves. The first half is due on or before November 30 and the second half on or before May 31 of the following year. Montana's Department of Revenue adds that the first payment is due November 30 or within 30 days of the postmark on your tax notice, whichever is later, and that a due date falling on a weekend or holiday moves to the next business day.

Residential property is valued every two years at 100 percent of market value. For tax year 2025 the state introduced a graduated rate for homes: 0.76 percent on the first $400,000 of market value, 1.10 percent on the portion between $400,000 and $1.5 million, and 2.20 percent above that. The Department of Revenue explains the tiers and notes that homeowners do not need to apply for them.

Unpaid taxes can eventually lead to a county tax deed sale. Butte-Silver Bow listed its next Tax Deed Auction for August 19, 2026, at 9:00 a.m. in the Council of Commissioners chambers. If you are behind on taxes, the amount is usually settled from your sale proceeds at closing, so ask the title company for a payoff figure early.

What does Montana law require a seller to disclose?

A Butte seller must give the buyer a written disclosure of adverse material facts the seller actually knows. Section 70-20-502 of the Montana Code requires the statement before or at the same time as the contract. It covers title problems, water and wastewater systems, utility connections, structural and mechanical systems, additions made without a building permit, hazardous materials, soil and drainage problems, and testing for asbestos, radon, lead-based paint, mold or contaminated soil.

If the statement arrives after a contract is signed, the buyer has three days to rescind in writing under section 70-20-504, unless the buyer waived that right in the offer. Some transfers are exempt, including those under a court order such as probate, foreclosure sales, transfers to a spouse, child or parent, transfers between co-owners, and sales where the buyer waived the statement in the contract (section 70-20-503).

What are your options for selling a house in Butte?

You can list with an agent, sell it yourself, or accept a cash offer. Each route trades time against price differently, and the right one depends on the condition of the house and how soon you need to close.

  • List with an agent. This can reach the widest group of buyers. It usually means showings, inspection requests and a buyer's lender, and a house with older systems may need repairs first.
  • Sell it yourself. You skip a listing commission but you handle marketing, paperwork and the disclosure statement alone.
  • Take a cash offer. A cash buyer purchases the house as it is. There is no lender appraisal, and the closing date is flexible. The offer reflects the condition of the house and the buyer's own costs, so compare it in writing against your net from a listing.

Whichever route you pick, get the net figure after taxes, liens, loan payoff and closing costs. That number, not the headline price, is what you actually take home.

What do Butte sellers usually run into?

  • Inherited houses with several heirs and an estate that has not closed.
  • Older Uptown properties where a financed buyer may ask for repairs before closing.
  • Vacant or neglected buildings where taxes have fallen behind.
  • Uncertainty about soil testing under the Superfund program.
  • Tenants in place on a rental the owner wants to be rid of.

More questions about Butte, MT

Do I have to fix my Butte house before I sell?

No. Montana law requires you to disclose known adverse material facts, not to repair them. A cash buyer purchases as-is, and a listing buyer may ask for repairs after an inspection.

Will the Butte Superfund lead cleanup stop me from selling?

No rule in the EPA's September 2026 amendment bars a sale. The amendment lowers the cleanup level to 456 ppm and expands the testing area, so a buyer may ask whether your property has been sampled. Contact the program about your address and disclose anything you know.

When are Butte-Silver Bow property taxes due?

Real estate taxes are due on or before November 30 and May 31. Check your notice, because the state allows the first payment to be due 30 days after the postmark if that is later.

What happens to unpaid property tax when I sell?

The title company normally pays the balance from your proceeds at closing. Ask for a payoff figure early so there are no surprises.

Is a seller disclosure statement required for an inherited house?

Transfers ordered by a probate court are exempt under section 70-20-503, and so are transfers to a spouse, child or parent of the owner. Other sales from an estate may still need the statement, so confirm with a title company or attorney.

What kind of city is Helena?

Helena is the capital of Montana and the county seat of Lewis and Clark County. The 2020 census counted 32,091 residents, which made it the sixth most populous city in the state and the fifth least populous state capital in the country. The Helena metro area, covering Lewis and Clark and Jefferson counties, had 83,058 people.

The city covers about 17 square miles and is served by Helena Regional Airport. It sits in the Helena Valley, with Tenmile Creek running through town and hillside neighborhoods rising on the edges. That hillside setting matters when you sell, because slopes, access roads and fire exposure are part of how a buyer sees a lot.

How did a gold camp become the state capital?

Helena began as a gold camp. Gold was found at Last Chance Gulch on July 14, 1864, and the town was formally established on October 30, 1864. The wealth of the early years left a mark on the housing stock: by 1888 about 50 millionaires lived in the area, and the concentration of money produced the elaborate Victorian architecture the city is known for.

Helena has been the capital of Montana Territory since 1875 and of the state since 1889, and voters kept it there in referendums in 1892 and 1894. The Montana State Capitol was completed in 1902. Downtown's walking mall follows the original path of Last Chance Gulch. It was built in the early 1980s after urban renewal removed many historic buildings from the downtown district.

Who employs people in Helena?

Government is the base of the local economy, and that tends to give Helena steadier employment than many Montana towns. Roughly 18 percent of working Helenans work for state government agencies, and the city is also a hub of county and federal activity. Education is a large employer too, with two high schools, their elementary and middle schools, and Helena College. Carroll College and the medical community are the major private employers listed for the city.

What does that mean for a seller? Buyers in Helena often have ties to government, schools or health care. An owner who relocates for work, retires or inherits a house from a parent often needs a predictable closing date, which is worth raising with any buyer.

What is Helena's climate, and how does it affect a house?

Helena has a semi-arid climate with long, cold winters, hot dry summers and short springs and autumns. Precipitation averages only 11.4 inches a year and mostly falls in spring. Snow can fall in any month except July but normally accumulates in light amounts, and chinook winds bring warm spells in winter.

The temperature range is wide. Helena has recorded 105 degrees Fahrenheit and a low of minus 42. With swings that wide, expect a buyer's inspector to look closely at the roof, siding and foundation.

Earthquakes are part of the local record as well. The 1935 Helena earthquake damaged the Broadwater Natatorium, which closed in 1941.

What do Helena's zoning rules say about fire, slopes and accessory units?

The city's zoning code states that its regulations seek to minimize danger from wildland fires, stormwater flooding, soil erosion and other environmental hazards, to mitigate traffic hazards and to protect the scenic character of hillside areas. Chapter 2 of Title 11 of the Helena City Code sets out the land uses allowed in each district.

The same chapter covers accessory dwelling units. An ADU is allowed accessory to a single-dwelling unit residence only, with one per lot. A detached or attached ADU cannot exceed 75 percent of the square footage of the main house or 1,000 square feet, whichever is less. If your property has a garage apartment or a converted basement, check with the city that it was permitted and fits these limits, because an unpermitted unit has to be disclosed.

Payments go to Lewis and Clark County at 316 North Park Avenue, Room 113, Helena, and the property tax office can be reached at 406-447-8329. Where is Kalispell and what does the name mean?

Kalispell is the county seat of Flathead County and the largest city in northwest Montana. The name is a Salish word meaning "flat land above the lake", and the lake is Flathead Lake, about 7 miles to the south. The city sits at an elevation of 3,084 feet and counted 24,558 residents in the 2020 census.

Kalispell is the commercial center of the Kalispell micropolitan area, and Wikipedia describes it as a secondary trade center with a trade area of approximately 130,000. U.S. Routes 93 and 2 cross in town. Glacier Park International Airport is about 8 miles northeast, between Kalispell and Columbia Falls, and Amtrak's Empire Builder stops in Whitefish, about 15 miles north.

Local transit is limited. Eagle Transit, run by the county, links Kalispell, Columbia Falls and Whitefish, but commuting in Flathead County is very car-dependent.

How was Kalispell founded?

Kalispell was a railroad town from the start. A short-lived settlement named Ashley appeared in 1884, and nearby Demersville grew quickly after 1887 until the Great Northern Railway bypassed it and people moved to the new town. The Kalispell Townsite Company, formed by Charles Edward Conrad and three Great Northern directors, platted the city, and lots were selling by the spring of 1891.

Kalispell was incorporated in 1892, and Conrad built a mansion there in 1895. The railroad later moved to a flatter route through Whitefish and Eureka in 1904, but the city kept growing. In 2018 the city bought and removed the long-abandoned track through town and relocated the railroad to the Glacier Rail Park, a new industrial park just north of town.

Who are the biggest employers around Kalispell?

Health care leads. The city's fiscal year 2019 financial report, as summarized on Wikipedia, ranked Logan Health Medical Center first with more than 1,000 employees. Weyerhaeuser had 500 to 999, and Health Center Northwest, Applied Materials, TeleTech, Glacier Bank, Whitefish Mountain Resort, Super 1 Foods, Walmart and Logan Health in Whitefish each had 250 to 499. That list is a few years old, so treat it as a guide to the mix of industries.

Logan Health describes its Medical Center as a 192-bed acute care regional referral center. Seasonal tourism around Whitefish Mountain Resort adds to the picture. For a seller, a hospital, a manufacturer and a resort suggest a mix of year-round and seasonal workers.

What is Kalispell's climate, and what does it do to a house?

Kalispell has a warm-summer humid continental climate with long, cold and moderately snowy winters and hot, dry summers. Snow usually falls from late October or early November through March. The airport's records since 1896 include a high of 105 degrees Fahrenheit, reached in August.

For a house, that means a roof that carries snow for five months, heating systems that run for a long season, and dry summers when yard and exterior upkeep matters. Be ready to tell a buyer the age of the roof and furnace.

How does Flathead County bill and collect property tax?

The Flathead County Treasurer collects the tax. The first half is due November 30 and becomes delinquent December 1, and the second half is due May 31 and becomes delinquent June 1. If a due date falls on a weekend or holiday, you can pay without penalty by 5:00 p.m. the next business day. The treasurer mails bills at least 30 days before November 30, and if a bill goes out later the taxpayer has 30 days from the postmark.

Owners of a primary residence can ask for an alternate schedule of seven monthly payments between November 30 and May 31 under section 15-16-122 of the Montana Code. The county says applications are due September 30 of the taxing year. If you plan to sell, a payment plan can help you stay current, and the unpaid balance is normally settled at closing.

State rules also apply. Residential property is valued every two years at 100 percent of market value. For tax year 2025, the rate on a home is 0.76 percent on the first $400,000 of market value, 1.10 percent from $400,000 to $1.5 million and 2.20 percent above that, as the Department of Revenue describes.

Do short-term rental and accessory unit rules affect a Kalispell sale?

They can, because the rules differ between the city and the surrounding county. Inside the city, the municipal code has short-term residential rental standards and accessory dwelling unit provisions, which appear in the city's ordinance disposition table. Outside the city limits, Flathead County has its own rules.

The county defines a short-term rental as a residential use in a dwelling designed for stays of less than 30 days. In most zoned areas, it requires an administrative conditional use permit. The review can take up to a month and a half and includes notice to every owner within 150 feet. Short-term rentals are permitted outright in some zones and not allowed in others, and in areas that are not zoned no permit is needed from Planning and Zoning.

If your house has been used as a vacation rental, a buyer will want to know whether the permit is in place and transferable. Ask the planning office before you list. A cash buyer may ask the same questions, so gather the paperwork first.

What must you tell a buyer in Montana?

  • Known problems with title or your ability to transfer the property.
  • Known issues with water, wells, wastewater or septic systems and utility connections.
  • Known structural, roof, foundation, plumbing, electrical or heating problems, and water intrusion.
  • Additions or alterations made without a building permit.
  • Hazardous materials, pests, soil or drainage problems, and any testing for radon, mold, lead-based paint or contaminated soil.

These items come from section 70-20-502 of the Montana Code, which requires the statement before or with the contract. If it arrives later, the buyer has three days to rescind under section 70-20-504, unless the buyer waived that right. Transfers under a court order, foreclosure sales, and transfers to a spouse, child or parent are exempt under section 70-20-503.

More questions about Kalispell, MT

When are Flathead County property taxes due?

The first half is due November 30 and the second half is due May 31. Unpaid amounts become delinquent on December 1 and June 1.

Can I pay my Kalispell property tax in monthly installments?

Owners of a primary residence can ask the Flathead County Treasurer for seven monthly payments between November 30 and May 31. Applications are due September 30 of the taxing year.

Do I need a permit to rent my Kalispell house short term?

In most zoned areas of Flathead County an administrative conditional use permit is required. Inside the city, check the municipal code or call the city's Development Services Department.

Do I have to disclose problems with my house in Montana?

Yes. You must disclose adverse material facts you actually know, in writing, before or with the contract. Some transfers, such as those ordered by a court, are exempt.

Can a cash buyer close without an inspection or a loan?

A cash buyer does not need a lender, so there is no loan approval or lender appraisal. Whether the buyer inspects the house is a term of the contract.
